descSub: ^\d+ Persian set phrases, idioms and proverbs, in three subdecks: \d+ everyday phrases, \d+ idioms and \d+ proverbs\.
{N} Persian set phrases, idioms and proverbs, in three subdecks: {SUB1} everyday phrases, {SUB2} idioms and {SUB3} proverbs.
Nothing here is taught by any of the five, so the two can be studied together without repeating an entry\.

Nothing here is taught by any of the five, so the two can be studied together without repeating an entry. WHEN TO START. The app deals the three subdecks side by side, and inside each the expressions now come by READING LEVEL: first those whose every word is a headword of Persian A1 or a form one of its cards shows ({A1PHRASES} phrases, {A1IDIOMS} idioms, {A1PROVERBS} proverbs), then those that need A2, B1, B2 and C1, then the ones with a word no level teaches. So the Phrases can be begun beside A1; the Idioms and the Proverbs are better left until B1. At the default pace of ten new cards a day the {N} expressions take {DAYS} days. TA'ÂROF. Persian politeness has a name, ta'ârof (تعارف): "an Iranian system of honour norms, a form of civility, or an art of etiquette, that emphasizes both deference and social rank" (Wikipedia, "Taarof", revision 1385845637): "In the rules of hospitality, taarof requires a host to offer anything a guest might want, and a guest is equally obliged to refuse it. This ritual may repeat itself several times (usually three times)" (the same article). Wiktionary marks one card here as its formula — قابل ندارد, "a kind of taarof commonly used by sellers" — and others are said in the same exchanges (وظیفه‌ام بود, it was my duty; زحمت نکشید; قدمت روی چشم); تعارف itself is a card of Persian B2, and بفرمایید, the word of every offer, is a card of Persian A1.

Within each subdeck the expressions come in the order of how many of Tatoeba's Persian sentences contain them, an expression ending in a verb being counted in any form of that verb; Tatoeba's Persian is small, so only 20 of the 106 are found there at all, and the rest follow in the order of how common their words are in film and television subtitles\.

persiana1.subtitle: {N} words · both directions, as two cards per word
descSub: \d[\d,]* words for a beginner
{N} words for a beginner
The Persian taught is the standard written language of Iran \(Farsi\), with the everyday spoken form shown beside a word where Tehran speech says it differently\.

WRITTEN AND SPOKEN PERSIAN ARE NOT THE SAME, and a beginner should know it from the first day. The cards teach the standard written language of Iran (Farsi); what is said in Tehran differs in regular ways — "When spoken formally, Iranian Persian is pronounced as written. But colloquial pronunciation as used by all classes makes a number of very common substitutions" (Wikipedia, "Persian phonology", revision 1386489168): ân is usually said un (نان nân, bread, is nun), است "is" is said -e, را is said ro or -o, the verb endings -id and -and are said -in and -an, and the commonest verbs are shortened (می‌خواهم mi-xâham, I want, is mixâm). A card shows the spoken form beside the written one, labelled "spoken", where the English Wiktionary gives it: on a word's own line (خانه, spoken خونه) and on a verb's, the forms for "I" and "he, she". The example sentences are mostly written Persian; a few are written the spoken way, as Tatoeba's contributors wrote them.

The first {HEAD} words are put by hand — the greetings and courtesies (سلام is the first card), a first exchange, the pronouns, twelve verbs, the words a sentence is built out of, the question words, zero to ten — and the rest follow by frequency, the words you meet most often first, with three sets each dealt whole and in order: the days of the week from Saturday, the first day of the Iranian week (from word {SET1}), the numbers above ten (from {SET2}) and the colours (from {SET3}).
